name: Zambia
summary: Formerly Northern Rhodesia, independent from Britain in 1964 under Kenneth Kaunda; one of Africa’s largest copper producers.

knownFor.label: Victoria Falls
knownFor.note: “The smoke that thunders”, shared with Zimbabwe.

terrain.value: A high plateau cut by the Zambezi River, with Victoria Falls on the border with Zimbabwe.

climate.value: Tropical but moderated by altitude, with a rainy season (November–April) and a dry season.

resources.value: Copper and cobalt, emeralds, hydropower from Kariba and Kafue, and farmland.

disasters.value: Droughts and floods; the 2015–16 drought cut hydropower output.

urbanisation.value: Lusaka is the capital; Kitwe and Ndola in the Copperbelt are major mining towns.

disease.value: HIV and malaria have been major problems, with progress in treatment since the 2000s.

migration.value: Many people moved to the Copperbelt for mining work, and rural-to-urban migration continues.

economicBase.value: Copper mining (698,000 metric tons in 2023) and farming.

tradeRoutes.value: The TAZARA railway (1975) links the Copperbelt to the Tanzanian port of Dar es Salaam, avoiding white-ruled Rhodesia.

wealth.value: A lower-middle-income country, still dependent on copper prices.

moneyAndTax.value: The kwacha (introduced 1968, replacing the Zambian pound); mining taxes are a big source of income.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A unitary presidential republic with a multi-party system.

keyRulers.value: Kenneth Kaunda (1964–91, lost the 1991 election), Frederick Chiluba (from 1991) and Michael Sata (2011–2014). Later and present leaders are not named here.

institutions.value: The National Assembly, an elected president and a court system based on English law.

stability.value: Peaceful since independence; one-party state under Kaunda from 1972 to 1991, then multiparty elections.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: A small army, air force and police, and a record of peaceful transfers of power.

majorWars.value: No wars of its own on the page. Kaunda backed Patriotic Front guerrillas raiding Rhodesia, and Zambia supported the ANC, which caused tensions and security problems. Angola and Mozambique are not mentioned in the part read.

territoryChange.value: The borders drawn in the colonial period have remained unchanged.

alliancesRivals.value: A “front-line state” against white-minority rule in Rhodesia, South Africa and Namibia, hosting liberation movements.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: The University of Zambia opened in 1966, soon after independence.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Railways run south to Zimbabwe and east to Tanzania; many roads connect the main towns.

religion.value: Sources differ: the infobox gives 95.5% Christian and the text cites 98.0% (2022). The 1991 declaration of a Christian nation is not covered in the part of the page read.

languageWriting.value: English is official; Bemba, Nyanja, Tonga and about 70 other languages are spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: Makishi masked dancers, Tonga basketry and Lozi royal festivals such as the Kuomboka.

socialStructure.value: About 70 ethnic groups and a growing urban middle class.

sharedIdentity.value: “One Zambia, one nation” was the national motto, to unite many ethnic groups.

dailyLife.value: Many families eat nshima (maize porridge) with relish and farm small plots or work in towns.

neighbours.value: DR Congo, Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Botswana, Namibia, Angola.

ideasReligions.value: Kenneth Kaunda’s Humanism, an African philosophy of socialism and cooperation, was the official ideology after independence.

colonisation.value: Known as Northern Rhodesia from 1911 to 1964, under British control.

riseSignals.value: Independence from the UK on 24 October 1964, as a republic within the Commonwealth.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge. The economy has long depended on copper, which was about 69% of export value in 2019.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still in existence: independent on 24 October 1964.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
